notes.short: “Go to Bethel and transgress”: said as a rebuke
notes.about: Through Amos the LORD seems to call Israel to keep up their worship at Bethel and Gilgal. He means the opposite. These words do not urge them to sin but rebuke them: their zealous offerings there were themselves rebellion, only added to their sin, and could not turn away His judgment (verse 12).

figure.name: Irony
figure.words: Go to Bethel and transgress; rebel even more at Gilgal!
figure.means: a rebuke, not a command: their worship at these shrines only multiplied their sin

original.note: In Hebrew “transgress” is pasha, to rebel or fall away, the verb used again in “rebel even more”: the call to worship is worded as a call to sin.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Amos 4:4-5 under Irony, plain from the close of the address in verse 12. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it bitter irony, the irony showing in the word for sin. Calvin says God speaks ironically in indignation, not to stir sinners on. Matthew Henry says it is spoken ironically. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) calls it irony: to multiply such service was to multiply transgression.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Divine Irony, p. 810
cites.quote: That this is Irony and sarcasm is clear from the conclusion of the address in verse 12.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: In bitter irony, Amos tells them to go on with zeal in their idolatrous sacrifices, and to multiply their sin. But they will not keep back the divine judgment by so doing. ... The irony of the summons to maintain their worship comes out very distinctly in the words וּפשׁעוּ, and sin, or fall away from God.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: It is the language of indignation; God indeed speaks ironically, and at the same time manifests his high displeasure, as though he had said, that they were wholly intractable, and could not be restrained by any corrections ... It is indeed certain, that God does not stimulate sinners; but he thus manifests his extreme indignation.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Come to Bethel, and transgress. It is spoken ironically: "Do so; take your course; multiply your transgressions by multiplying your sacrifices, for this liketh you; but what will you do in the end hereof?"
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Having foretold their captivity, the prophet tries irony. But his irony is in bidding them go on to do, what they were doing earnestly, what they were set upon doing, and would not be withdrawn from. ... so Amos bids them do all they did, in their divided service of God, but tells them that to multiply all such service was to multiply transgression.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Three sins, then four: sin piled on sin
notes.about: The LORD speaks of three transgressions of Damascus, then four. The numbers are not a count: they tell of sin added to sin, so that the LORD will not revoke His judgment. The same saying opens each of the eight charges, from Damascus to Israel (Amos 2:6).

figure.name: Numerical saying
figure.words: three transgressions of Damascus, even four
figure.means: many sins, one added to another, until the judgment can no longer be turned back

notes.evidence: Henry reads three or four as many, or as seven, the measure filled up. Calvin takes the numbers for the many sins and stubborn perverseness of Damascus; Clarke, for abundance; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), for sin on sin; Keil (Keil and Delitzsch), for many sins, the exact count of no matter. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) sees one sin beyond, by which a full measure overflows.
notes.limit: The writers agree the numbers are not a count. Some read them simply as many sins; others see the last as the sin that makes a full measure overflow, or the two together as seven, a full number.

cites.quote: they are charged in general with three transgressions, and with four, that is, with many transgressions (as by one or two we mean a few, so by three or four we mean many ... or with three and four, that is, with seven transgressions, a number of perfection, intimating that they have filled up the measure of their iniquities
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: the most suitable sense here is that for the many sins of Damascus God would not be propitious to it: and the Prophet, I have no doubt, intended by the two numbers to set forth the irreclaimable perverseness of the Syrians.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: These expressions of three and four, so often repeated in this chapter, mean repetition, abundance, and any thing that goes towards excess.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: If Damascus had only sinned once or twice, I would have spared them, but since, after having been so often pardoned, they still persevere so continually, I will no longer "turn away" their punishment. ... "Three and four" imply sin multiplied on sin
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In the formula, which is repeated in the case of every people, "for three transgressions, and for four," the numbers merely serve to denote the multiplicity of the sins, the exact number of which has no bearing upon the matter.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: These words express, not four transgressions added to the three, but an additional transgression beyond the former, the last sin, whereby the measure of sin, which before was full, overflows, and God's wrath comes. So in other places, where the like form of words occurs, the added number is one beyond, and mostly relates to something greater than all the rest.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Five times: “yet you did not return to Me”
notes.about: Five times the LORD names a hardship He sent on Israel: famine, drought, blight and locusts, plague and the sword, and an overthrow like that of Sodom. Each time the same words close it. They show how patiently He called His people back, and how they would not come.

lines.words: yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD.
yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD.
yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD.
yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD.
yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD.

original.note: In Hebrew the five lines are word for word the same, ve-lo shavtem adai, from shuv, the verb for turning back.

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the words, repeated five times, show the Lord’s unwearied love to His rebellious children, and Bullinger lists the five as a refrain. Henry calls them the burden of the charge. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the same sad result is added to each chastisement, marking their obstinacy, and Clarke finds in them God's longsuffering.

cites.quote: This last thought is explained in Amo 4:6-11 in a series of instances, in which the expression ולא שׁבתּם עדי (and ye have not returned to me), which is repeated five times, depicts in the most thorough manner the unwearied love of the Lord to His rebellious children.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Here we have the solemn refrain five times repeated “Yet have ye not returned unto me saith the Lord.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: It is five times repeated in these verses, as the burden of the charge, "Yet have you not returned unto me, saith the Lord; you have been several times corrected, but in vain; you are not reclaimed, there is no sign of amendment. You have been sent for by one messenger after another, but you have not come back, you have not come home."
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Jehovah details His several chastisements inflicted with a view to reclaiming them: but adds to each the same sad result, "yet have ye not returned unto Me" ... the monotonous repetition of the same burden marking their pitiable obstinacy.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This reprehension is repeated ... in this chapter; and in it are strongly implied God's longsuffering, his various modes of fatherly chastisement, the ingratitude of the people, and their obstinate wickedness.

notes.short: Two lines, one famine: clean teeth and no bread
notes.about: The second line says the first again in plainer words. Teeth left clean in all the cities are explained by lack of bread in all the towns: both lines tell of famine, the first of the hardships the LORD sent to call Israel back.

lines.words: I beset all your cities with cleanness of teeth
and all your towns with lack of bread,

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) and Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) both say cleanness of teeth is explained by the parallel line, lack of bread. H. R. Reynolds and O. C. Whitehouse (Ellicott's Commentary) say the poetic parallelism makes the two one, Calvin says Amos explains his own figure by want of bread, and Clarke takes it as scarcity of bread, as the next words explain.

cites.quote: Cleanness of teeth is explained by the parallel "want of bread." The first chastisement, therefore, consisted in famine
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: cleanness of teeth--explained by the parallel, "want of bread."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Cleanness of teeth is, by the poetic parallelism, identified with the want of bread
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: It is a figurative expression, by which Amos means want, and he explains it himself by want of bread

cites.quote: Cleanness of teeth - Scarcity of bread, as immediately explained. Ye shall have no trouble in cleaning your teeth, for ye shall have nothing to eat.
